title: Supervisory Stress Test Documentation Final 2026 Global Market Shock Component
summary: The Federal Reserve Board released the final documentation for the 2026 Supervisory Stress Test Global Market Shock (GMS) component, describing the hypothetical shocks to financial risk factors—including equities, currencies, commodities, interest rates, and credit—used in the severely adverse scenario. Firms subject to the GMS are those with $50 billion or more in aggregate trading assets and liabilities, or trading activities equal to 10% or more of total consolidated assets. The 2025 stress test used an as-of date of October 11, 2024.
key_points: Global Market Shock applies to firms with aggregate trading assets and liabilities of $50 billion or more, or 10% or more of total consolidated assets
Losses from the global market shock are recognized in the first quarter of the scenario horizon with no changes assumed in subsequent quarters
Risk factors include public equity returns from advanced and emerging economies, exchange rates, government yields, implied volatilities, commodity futures, and credit spreads
The GMS is applied to positions held on the as-of date (e.g., October 11, 2024 for the 2025 cycle), which may differ from the year-end macroeconomic scenario date
This document finalizes the October 2025 proposal with only typographical corrections; the Board proposed changes to the as-of date in its Enhanced Transparency proposal
Stress test scenarios are explicitly not forecasts—they are hypothetical paths for assessing capital resilience
why_it_matters: This technical documentation defines how the Federal Reserve models severe but hypothetical market dislocations for bank stress testing purposes. It establishes the methodology that determines trading-related capital losses under adverse conditions for major U.S. financial institutions, directly affecting how banks must prepare for regulatory capital assessments.
market_structure_context: The GMS component provides a standardized framework for applying simultaneous shocks across multiple asset classes (equities, FX, rates, commodities, credit) to assess market-wide stress impacts on trading books. It models relationships between primary risk factors, secondary factors, and remaining risk factors, reflecting interconnected market dynamics during financial distress.
important_numbers: October 11, 2024 as-of date for 2025 stress test
notes: Source is a technical methodology PDF document rather than a news article or policy announcement. While it defines market stress parameters for regulatory purposes, it does not represent a live market catalyst. Published February 2026, making it recent. Document is comprehensive but the source body was truncated; additional detail on specific risk factor calibrations may exist beyond the visible text.
